title: Father of six killed by police
article: Howard Fleury, 34, was shot just before midnight inside his home at 339 Alfred Ave., and later died in hospital.
Police did not release the man's name yesterday, but he was identified by relatives.

At least some of Fleury's six children and two grandchildren were on the snow-covered lawn with their mother when police entered the home just before the deadly altercation, said a spokesman with the Manitoba Métis Federation, who was contacted because the victim was Métis.
Patrol Sgt. Kelly Dennison said the homicide unit is investigating Fleury's death.
"This confrontation escalated to the point where the male was shot by police," Dennison said. "There will be a full investigation."
Police treat fatal police shootings as homicide investigations, gathering forensic evidence and witness statements.
Dennison would not release any information on what steps police took before using deadly force.
Dennison would not say how many shots were fired, what part of the body the man was hit, or any information on the officer or officers involved.
"We will release more, but we have to give our officers more time and the family more time," Dennison said.
The officers involved were immediately placed on three days' administrative leave, Dennison said.
Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand told the Free Press he heard that pepper spray was used by officers when they entered the home.
Chartrand, who was contacted by police early yesterday morning, said he was also told the man, believed to be intoxicated, was shot four times.
It is the second time city police have shot a person this year.
Matthew Dumas, 18, was killed on Dufferin Avenue on Jan. 31.
An internal police investigation recommended criminal charges not be laid against the officer who shot and killed the man, who was armed with a screwdriver and was advancing on police.
Police are allowed to use deadly force if they believe their lives or the lives of others are in danger.
Under police use-of-force guidelines, they are permitted to use a level of force one step above the threat before them.

"Officers go through a lot of training to address situations without using lethal force," Dennison said. "But we all took an oath, and you realize that you may be forced one day to make a decision to use lethal force."
Fleury's mother, Barbara Fleury, told the Free Press she has questions about her son's death.
"What I don't understand is why they didn't shoot him in the leg or something," she said, wiping away tears.
Officers arrived at her cramped basement apartment in the West End just before 6 a.m. yesterday morning to tell her Howard was dead.

The police have shared few details with her about what happened Friday night, but she said they told her they arrived at his home on a domestic disturbance call and found the man's common-law wife, Kimberly Deslarlais, outside with some of the couple's six children.
"Howard opened the door, saw the police officers and went back inside," Fleury said. "The police followed. Something happened inside the house."

Yesterday afternoon, Fleury flipped through family photo albums, pausing to look at shots of Howard smiling, flanked by children. While she wept, Howard's father, Leonard, stood silently against the wall.
She finds it difficult to imagine her son brandishing a weapon at police.
"Everyone said it. He's mellow, he is shy-like, he's quiet," Barbara Fleury said. "He was happy-go-lucky with me."
Fleury said she doesn't have any reason to believe her son's Métis heritage has anything to do with his death.
Chartrand, who was in Saskatoon at the time of the shooting, said police advised him about it at 5 a.m. yesterday.
"Police indicated that when they entered the house, something went wrong," he said. "There was pepper spray involved, and then something went wrong.
"Mr. Fleury had a knife, and I guess he reacted in a forceful way and police, feeling their life was threatened, then utilized their weapons."
Chartrand said he has talked with Fleury's family and assured them he would find out if the shooting was justified.
He said he wasn't about to jump to any conclusions. "Police today are so cautious... they have to be," he said. "So, that's why it's hard to just say, 'Hey, they shouldn't have shot him.'
"Society in general has changed so much. There is so much death. Someone gets shot so easily now," Chartrand added. "It's forcing a different style of policing now.
"But at the same time, we have to ensure they don't use lethal force if they don't have to. We have to make sure everything was followed according to procedure."
Chartrand commended the police for advising him of the tragedy.
"It's a very positive step... advising us what took place and promising to keep us up to speed."
The MMF's Child and Family Support Service staff are helping the man's family cope with their loss, ensuring they have groceries and clothing while they stay with relatives.
Chartrand said he expects the children will be traumatized.
"We believe they saw what happened... we have support staff working with them right now," he said.
Patrol Sgt. Dennison said officers at the scene are also receiving support from the Winnipeg Police Service.
"They'll receive as much help as we can provide," he said. "It does affect every police officer, no doubt about it."
Howard Fleury, born in Prince Albert and raised in Winnipeg, was one of four brothers.
According to his mother, he and Deslarlais had been together since he was 15 and had six children, the oldest in her late teens.
Barbara Fleury said she was estranged from the family because she and Deslarlais didn't get along, but she did keep in contact with her son.
Fleury said her son was working at a furniture store and renting the home on Alfred.
The freshly painted grey and white home has a new porch wrapped in garland. A Santa Claus poster covers the front door and oversized snowflakes decorate the windows.
"It's going to be one sad Christmas for that family," Chartrand said.
Neighbours say the family had only been living there less than two months and they never noticed any trouble at the home.

Neighbour Barb Christie said she often saw young children playing in the home's yard. But she never noticed any trouble with police until Friday night, when she woke up to lights and sirens and watched paramedics roll a man out of the home on a gurney.
Another neighbour, Angela Schaefer, said police should have tried to just wound him.
City police are not trained to wound; they are trained to shoot at the centre of the attacker's body.
